﴿And He will admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾: The manner of the rivers flowing beneath the gardens has already been explained. ﴿And pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence﴾: that is, in gardens of lasting abode. ﴿That is the great achievement﴾: that is, the mentioned forgiveness and the admission into the described gardens is the achievement after which there is no further achievement, and the triumph to which none is comparable.

﴿And [there is] another [favor] you love﴾

Al-Akhfash and al-Farraʾ said: "ukhrā" (another) is in conjunction with "tijarah" (transaction), so it is in the genitive position; that is, "shall I guide you to another quality you love, in this world along with the reward of the Hereafter?" It was also said it is in the nominative position, meaning "and for you is another quality," and it was said it is in the accusative position, meaning "and He will give you another quality."

Then Allah, glorified is He, explained this other [favor], saying: ﴿victory from Allah and an imminent conquest﴾: that is, it is victory from Allah for you and an imminent conquest.

Al-Kalbi said: it means victory over Quraysh and the conquest of Makkah.

ʿAta' said: it means the conquest of Persia and Byzantium. ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ is conjoined to an omitted element, meaning: say, O you who have believed, and give good tidings; or it is conjoined to "tuʾminūna," since it has the meaning of a command. The meaning is: give good tidings, O Muhammad, to the believers of victory and conquest; or give them good tidings of victory in this world and conquest, and of Paradise in the Hereafter; or give them good tidings of Paradise in the Hereafter.

Then Allah, glorified is He, urged the believers to support His religion, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, be helpers of Allah﴾: that is, persist in what you are upon of supporting the religion.

Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Nafi' recited "anṣāran lillāh" with tanwin and without the idafah (construct). The rest recited with the idafah. The orthography admits both readings together, and Abu ʿUbayd chose the reading with idafah because of His saying ﴿We are helpers of Allah﴾ with the idafah.

﴿As Jesus, the son of Mary, said to the disciples, "Who are my helpers for Allah?"﴾: that is, support the religion of Allah in the manner of the support of the disciples when Jesus said to them, "Who are my helpers for Allah?" They said, "We are helpers of Allah." The kaf in "kamā qāla" is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, its estimate being: "be a being like what he said." It was also said the kaf is in the accusative position by an implied verb. It was also said it is a statement carried on its meaning rather than its wording, and the meaning is: be helpers of Allah as the disciples were helpers of Jesus when he said to them, "Who are my helpers for Allah?"

His saying ﴿ilā Allāh﴾ (for Allah): it was said "ilā" has the meaning of "maʿa" (with), that is, "who are my helpers with Allah?" It was said the estimate is: "who are my helpers in what brings one closer to Allah?" It was said the estimate is: "who are my helpers heading toward the support of Allah?" The discussion of this has already preceded in Surat Al ʿImran.

The disciples (al-Hawariyyun) were the helpers of the Messiah and his pure companions, and the first to believe in him; their description has already preceded.

﴿So a faction of the Children of Israel believed and a faction disbelieved﴾: that is, a faction believed in Jesus and a faction disbelieved in him. That was because, when they differed after his raising, they separated and fought. ﴿Then We supported those who believed against their enemy﴾: that is, We strengthened the righteous among them against the falsifiers. ﴿So they became dominant﴾: that is, high and victorious. It was said the meaning is: We then supported the Muslims against both factions together.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: They said, "If only we knew which deeds are most beloved to Allah!" So there was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ They disliked it, so there was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ up to His saying: ﴿a solid structure﴾.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, be helpers of Allah﴾ that he said: "That has already occurred, praise be to Allah. Seventy men came to him, pledged allegiance to him at al-ʿAqabah, sheltered him and supported him, until Allah made His religion prevail."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Saʿd narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAmr ibn Hazm, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the group who met him at al-ʿAqabah: 'Bring out to me twelve of you who will be guarantors over their people, as the disciples were guarantors for Jesus, son of Mary.'"

Ibn Saʿd narrated from Mahmud ibn Labid, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the chiefs (nuqabaʾ): 'You are guarantors over your people, like the guarantee of the disciples for Jesus, son of Mary, and I am the guarantor of my people.' They said: 'Yes.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿So We supported those who believed﴾ that he said: "We strengthened those who believed." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him: ﴿So We supported those who believed with Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community against their enemy, so they became dominant today.﴾

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 61, verses 1–14 (part 1 of 2):

It is Madani (revealed in Medina).
Al-Mawardi said: this is the view of the majority.
Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surat al-Saff was revealed in Medina."
Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.
Al-Nahhas narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surat al-Saff was revealed in Mecca." Perhaps this is not authentic from him. What supports its being Madani is what Ahmad narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, who said: "We were discussing among ourselves which of us would go to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and ask him: 'Which deeds are most beloved to Allah?' None of us stood up. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent for us one by one and gathered us, and he recited to us this surah, meaning Surat al-Saff, in its entirety." Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated it, and said at its end: "So this surah was revealed concerning them."
al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim also narrated it, and al-Hakim said: "Sahih according to the criteria of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim)." al-Bayhaqi also narrated it in al-Shuʿab and al-Sunan.

(p-1487) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah﴾: this has already been discussed. The reason some surahs use the present tense and others the imperative is to direct attention to the legitimacy of glorifying (tasbih) at all times, past, future and present, and we have already mentioned something similar at the beginning of Surat al-Hadid. ﴿And He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾: al-ʿAziz means the Overpowering who cannot be overpowered, and al-Hakim means the Wise in His acts and His words.

﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ This interrogative is for reproach and rebuke, meaning: why do you say good things that you do not do? "Lima" is composed of the preposition lam (li-) and the interrogative "ma," and its alif was dropped for lightness because of its frequent use, as in its counterparts.

Then He, glorified is He, censured them for this, saying: ﴿Greatly hateful in the sight of Allah is that you say what you do not do﴾. That is: this is greatly abhorrent in terms of hatred (maqt), which is aversion. Al-maqt and al-maqatah are both verbal nouns. It is said: "a man is maqit and mamqut" when people do not love him. Al-Kisa'i said: "an tqulu" is in the position of nominative, because "kabura" is a verb with the meaning of "baisa" (how wretched), and "maqtan" is accusative as a specification (tamyiz). On this view, "kabura" contains an ambiguous pronoun explained by the indefinite noun, and "an taqulu" is the subject of the dispraise. There arises the disagreement over whether its nominative is by inception (mubtada'), with its predicate being the sentence preceding it, or whether its predicate is omitted, or whether it is the predicate of an omitted subject.

If it were said that by his saying "kabura" he intended amazement (ta'ajjub), Ibn ʿUsfur counted it among the verbs of amazement.
It was also said that it is neither a verb of dispraise nor a verb of amazement, but rather it is predicated of "an taqulu," and "maqtan" is a specification transferred from the agent.

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row, as if they were a solid structure﴾: The commentators said: the believers said, "We wish that Allah would inform us of the deeds most beloved to Him so that we may do them, even if our wealth and our lives are lost in them." So Allah revealed ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight﴾ and so on. "Saffan" is accusative as a verbal noun, and the object is omitted, meaning: they arrange themselves in a row. It was also said that it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: lined up or arranged.

The majority read "yuqatilun" with the active voice. Zayd ibn ʿAli read it in the passive voice. It was also read "yaqtulun" with a shadda. The clause ﴿as if they were a solid structure﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of "yuqatilun," or to the pronoun in "saffan," on the assumption that it is interpreted as "lined up" or "arranged." The meaning of "marsus" is: adhering to one another; it is said, "I laid the building, I lay it with laying (rassan)," when one joins its parts to one another. Al-Farra' said: "marsus" means "with lead" (al-rasas). Al-Mubarrad said: it is derived from "I laid the building" when I plastered between its parts and brought them close until it became like a single piece. It was also said: it is from al-rasis, which is joining things to one another; and al-tarassus means adhering closely.

﴿And when Musa said to his people﴾: When He, glorified is He, mentioned that He loves those who fight in His cause, He made clear that Musa and ʿIsa commanded monotheism, strove in the cause of Allah, and punishment befell those who opposed them. The adverbial phrase is connected to an omitted verb which is "udhkur" (remember), meaning: remember, O Muhammad, for these averse people, the time when Musa spoke. It is possible that the reason for mentioning the story of Musa and ʿIsa after the love of those who strive in the cause of Allah is to warn the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) not to do with their Prophet what the people of Musa and ʿIsa did with them both. ﴿O my people, why do you harm me?﴾ This is the content of the saying: why do you harm me by opposing what I command you of the laws which Allah has made obligatory upon you? Or: why do you harm me with insults and disparagement? Among this is their accusation against him of having the "udra" (a swelling of the testicles), and the explanation of this has already been given in Surat al-Ahzab. The clause ﴿and you know that I am the Messenger of Allah to you﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, and "qad" is for the certainty of knowledge or for its emphasis. The present form signifies continuity, and the meaning is: how do you harm me while you know that I am the Messenger of Allah? A messenger is to be respected and honored, and there remains with you no doubt about the message, because of the miracles you have witnessed, which oblige you to acknowledge my message and give you certain knowledge of it.

﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾: That is, when they persisted in deviation and continued upon it, Allah caused their hearts to deviate from guidance and turned them away from accepting the truth. It was also said: when they deviated from faith, Allah caused their hearts to deviate from reward.
Muqatil said: when they turned away from the truth, Allah inclined their hearts away from it, meaning that when they abandoned the truth by harming their Prophet, Allah inclined their hearts away from the truth as a recompense for what they had committed. ﴿And Allah does not guide the corrupt people﴾: this sentence confirms the content of what precedes it.
al-Zajjaj said: He does not guide those whom it has been foreknown in His knowledge are corrupt. The meaning is that He does not guide every person characterized by corruption, and these are among them.

﴿And when ʿIsa, son of Maryam, said﴾: This is coordinated with "and when Musa said," and is governed by its own governing element, or by an omitted governing element coordinated with the governing element of the first temporal adverb.
﴿O Children of Israel, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah﴾: That is, I am the Messenger of Allah to you with the Gospel, confirming what came before me of the Torah, because I have not brought you anything that contradicts the Torah; rather it contains good tidings of me. So how can you turn away from me and oppose me? "Musaddiqan" is accusative as a circumstantial clause, and likewise "mubashshiran," and the governing element in both is the sense of sending contained in "rasul." The meaning is: I have been sent to you while confirming what came before me of the Torah and giving good tidings of one who comes after me. Since I am such in confirming and giving good tidings, there is no reason for you to deny me. "Ahmad" is the name of our Prophet (ﷺ), and it is a proper name derived from the adjective. It may be an intensive form of the active participle, meaning that he is more praising of Allah than others, or of the passive participle, meaning that he is praised for the good qualities within him more than others are praised.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, al-Sulami, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿min baʿdi﴾ with a fatha on the ya'. The rest read it with a sukun.

﴿So when he came to them with clear proofs, they said, "This is manifest magic"﴾: That is, when ʿIsa came to them with miracles, they said, "This which he has brought us is manifest, clear magic." It was also said that the intended person is Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning that when he came to them with that, they uttered this statement, and the first is preferable.

The majority read ﴿siḥrun﴾ (magic). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "sahir" (sorcerer).

﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents falsehood against Allah while he is being invited to Islam?﴾: That is, there is no one more unjust than him, since he fabricates lies against Allah while being invited to the religion of Islam, which is the best and most noble of religions. For whoever is in this condition, it is his duty not to fabricate falsehood against others, so how could he fabricate it against his Lord?

The majority read ﴿wa-huwa yudʿa﴾ from "du'a'" (invitation), in the passive voice. Talhah ibn Musarrif read "yaddaʿi" with a fatha on the ya' and a shadda on the dal, from "ida'" (claim), in the active voice. It takes "ila" because it is implicitly construed with the meaning of affiliation and belonging. ﴿And Allah does not guide the unjust people﴾: this sentence confirms the content of what precedes it. The meaning is: He does not guide one who is characterized by injustice, and those mentioned are among them.

﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths﴾: Ițfa' (extinguishing) means quenching, and its origin is with fire; it is used figuratively for what is similar to it in terms of becoming manifest. By "the light of Allah" is meant the Qur'an, meaning: they wish to nullify it and deny it by speech; or Islam; or Muhammad (ﷺ); or the proofs and evidences; or all of what has been mentioned. The meaning of "with their mouths" is: with their statements issuing from their mouths, containing reproach. ﴿But Allah will perfect His light﴾ by making it manifest throughout the horizons and elevating it above others.

Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿mutimmu nurihi﴾ with the genitive construction (idafa), and the rest read "mutimmun" with tanwin. ﴿Although the disbelievers dislike it﴾: that is, it is certainly going to happen, and the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: the lam in ﴿li-yuṭfi'ū﴾ is an emphatic lam which has entered upon the object, because the underlying form is "they wish that they extinguish." This lam is most often required when the object is fronted, as in your saying, "Lazaydun darabtu" and "Lirru'yatuka qasadtu." It was also said that it is the lam of cause, and the object is omitted, meaning: they wish to nullify the Qur'an, or to repel Islam, or to kill the Messenger, in order that they may extinguish. It was also said that it is in the sense of "an" (that), which is itself the governing particle.

al-Farra' said: the Arabs make the lam of "kay" (in order that) in the position of "an" after "arada" (wished) and "amara" (commanded). Al-Kisa'i went to this view, and similar to this is His saying: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 26].

The sentence ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, to make it prevail over all religion, even though the polytheists dislike it﴾ is a resumptive sentence confirming what precedes it. "Al-huda" is the Qur'an or the miracles. The meaning of "the religion of truth" is the true creed, which is the creed of Islam. The meaning of "li-yuzhirahu" is: to make it manifest over all religions, dominant over them and prevailing over them. ﴿Although the polytheists dislike it﴾: that is certainly going to happen.

Mujahid said: this will be when ʿIsa descends; there will be no religion on the earth except the religion of Islam. "Din" is a verbal noun used to refer to the many religions. The apodosis of "law" in both places is omitted, and the estimated reading is: He will perfect it and make it manifest.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Some of the believers, before jihad was enjoined, used to say: "We wish that Allah would inform us of the deeds most beloved to Him so that we may act upon it." So Allah informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that the most beloved deed is faith in Allah without doubt, and striving against the people of His disobedience who opposed faith and did not acknowledge it. When fighting was enjoined, some of the believers disliked it and found its command difficult, so Allah said: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿Greatly hateful in the sight of Allah is that you say what you do not do﴾, that he said: this verse concerns fighting alone, and they were people who used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and a man would say, "I fought and struck with my sword," when they had not done so; so this was revealed.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him, who said: They said, "If we knew the deeds most beloved to Allah, we would do them." So Allah informed them, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row, as if they were a solid structure﴾. They disliked that, so Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ and ﴿Greatly hateful in the sight of Allah is that you say what you do not do.﴾

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: ﴿as if they were a solid structure﴾, he said: firmly established, not moving, its parts joined closely to one another.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 61, verses 1–14 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I have names: I am Muhammad, I am Ahmad, I am al-Hashir (the Gatherer) at whose feet Allah will gather the people, I am al-Mahi (the Eraser) through whom Allah erases disbelief, and I am al-Aqib (the Last), after whom there is no prophet.'"

﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ ﴿You believe in Allah and His Messenger and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives. That is best for you, if you only knew.﴾ ﴿He will forgive you your sins and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence. That is the great achievement.﴾ ﴿And [there is] another [favor] you love: victory from Allah and an imminent conquest. So give good tidings to the believers.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, be helpers of Allah, as Jesus, the son of Mary, said to the disciples, "Who are my helpers for Allah?" The disciples said, "We are helpers of Allah." So a faction of the Children of Israel believed, and a faction disbelieved. Then We supported those who believed against their enemy, and they became dominant.﴾

His saying ﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾: He made the mentioned action equivalent to a transaction, because they profit from it just as they profit from trade, namely by their entry into Paradise and their deliverance from the Fire.

The majority of readers recited ﴿tunjikum﴾ (will save you) with light stress, from al-injaʾ (deliverance). Al-Hasan, Ibn ʿAmir and Abu Haywah recited it with emphatic stress, from al-tanjiyah.

Then Allah, glorified is He, explained this transaction to which He had pointed, saying: ﴿You believe in Allah and His Messenger and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives.﴾ This is a statement in the sense of a command, to indicate the obligation of compliance, so it is as though it has already occurred, and so He informed of its occurrence. He placed mention of wealth before lives because it is that with which one begins in spending and in preparing for jihad.

The majority recited ﴿tuʾminūna﴾ (you believe), while Ibn Masʿud recited: "Āminū wa-jāhidū" (believe and strive), in the imperative.

Al-Akhfash said: ﴿tuʾminūna﴾ is a explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayān) to "tijarah" (transaction). The better view is that the clause is a new sentence (mustaʾnafah) explaining what precedes it. The demonstrative in His saying ﴿dhālikum﴾ (that) refers to the mentioned belief and jihad; it is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿khayrun lakum﴾ (is best for you), meaning: this act is better for you than your wealth and your lives. ﴿If you [only] knew﴾ means: if you are among those who know, for you would know that it is best for you; not if you are of the people of ignorance, for then you would not know that.

﴿He will forgive you your sins﴾: This is the answer to the command implied by the wording of the statement, and for this reason it is in the jussive mood.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Mubarrad said: His saying ﴿tuʾminūna﴾ has the meaning of "āminū" (believe!), and for this reason ﴿yaghfir lakum﴾ (He will forgive you) came in the jussive mood.

Al-Farraʾ said: ﴿yaghfir lakum﴾ is the answer to the interrogative, so he made it jussive because it is the answer to the interrogative. The scholars have considered this an error.

Al-Zajjaj said: When He directs them to what benefits them, it is not that He forgives them; rather He forgives them when they believe and strive.

Al-Razi, in explaining al-Farraʾ's view, said: "Hal adullukum" (shall I guide you?) has the meaning of a command in his view, as one says "Hal anta sakit?" (Are you silent?), meaning "be silent!" Its explanation is that "hal" has the meaning of interrogation, then it gradually becomes an offer and an urging, and urging is like incitement, and incitement is a command.

Zayd ibn ʿAli recited "tuʾminū, wa-tujāhidū" (believe and strive), with the imperative particle lam elided and understood.

It was also said: "yaghfir lakum" is jussive by an implied condition, meaning: if you believe, He will forgive you. Some recited with assimilation (idgham) in ﴿yaghfir lakum﴾, but the better course is to omit assimilation, because the rāʾ is a repeated letter, so it is not good to assimilate it into the lām.

﴿And He will admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾: The manner of the rivers flowing beneath the gardens has already been explained. ﴿And pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence﴾: that is, in gardens of lasting abode. ﴿That is the great achievement﴾: that is, the mentioned forgiveness and the admission into the described gardens is the achievement after which there is no further achievement, and the triumph to which none is comparable.

﴿And [there is] another [favor] you love﴾

Al-Akhfash and al-Farraʾ said: "ukhrā" (another) is in conjunction with "tijarah" (transaction), so it is in the genitive position; that is, "shall I guide you to another quality you love, in this world along with the reward of the Hereafter?" It was also said it is in the nominative position, meaning "and for you is another quality," and it was said it is in the accusative position, meaning "and He will give you another quality."

Then Allah, glorified is He, explained this other [favor], saying: ﴿victory from Allah and an imminent conquest﴾: that is, it is victory from Allah for you and an imminent conquest.

Al-Kalbi said: it means victory over Quraysh and the conquest of Makkah.

ʿAta' said: it means the conquest of Persia and Byzantium. ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ is conjoined to an omitted element, meaning: say, O you who have believed, and give good tidings; or it is conjoined to "tuʾminūna," since it has the meaning of a command. The meaning is: give good tidings, O Muhammad, to the believers of victory and conquest; or give them good tidings of victory in this world and conquest, and of Paradise in the Hereafter; or give them good tidings of Paradise in the Hereafter.

Then Allah, glorified is He, urged the believers to support His religion, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, be helpers of Allah﴾: that is, persist in what you are upon of supporting the religion.

Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Nafi' recited "anṣāran lillāh" with tanwin and without the idafah (construct). The rest recited with the idafah. The orthography admits both readings together, and Abu ʿUbayd chose the reading with idafah because of His saying ﴿We are helpers of Allah﴾ with the idafah.

﴿As Jesus, the son of Mary, said to the disciples, "Who are my helpers for Allah?"﴾: that is, support the religion of Allah in the manner of the support of the disciples when Jesus said to them, "Who are my helpers for Allah?" They said, "We are helpers of Allah." The kaf in "kamā qāla" is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, its estimate being: "be a being like what he said." It was also said the kaf is in the accusative position by an implied verb. It was also said it is a statement carried on its meaning rather than its wording, and the meaning is: be helpers of Allah as the disciples were helpers of Jesus when he said to them, "Who are my helpers for Allah?"

His saying ﴿ilā Allāh﴾ (for Allah): it was said "ilā" has the meaning of "maʿa" (with), that is, "who are my helpers with Allah?" It was said the estimate is: "who are my helpers in what brings one closer to Allah?" It was said the estimate is: "who are my helpers heading toward the support of Allah?" The discussion of this has already preceded in Surat Al ʿImran.

The disciples (al-Hawariyyun) were the helpers of the Messiah and his pure companions, and the first to believe in him; their description has already preceded.

﴿So a faction of the Children of Israel believed and a faction disbelieved﴾: that is, a faction believed in Jesus and a faction disbelieved in him. That was because, when they differed after his raising, they separated and fought. ﴿Then We supported those who believed against their enemy﴾: that is, We strengthened the righteous among them against the falsifiers. ﴿So they became dominant﴾: that is, high and victorious. It was said the meaning is: We then supported the Muslims against both factions together.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: They said, "If only we knew which deeds are most beloved to Allah!" So there was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ They disliked it, so there was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ up to His saying: ﴿a solid structure﴾.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, be helpers of Allah﴾ that he said: "That has already occurred, praise be to Allah. Seventy men came to him, pledged allegiance to him at al-ʿAqabah, sheltered him and supported him, until Allah made His religion prevail."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Saʿd narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAmr ibn Hazm, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the group who met him at al-ʿAqabah: 'Bring out to me twelve of you who will be guarantors over their people, as the disciples were guarantors for Jesus, son of Mary.'"

Ibn Saʿd narrated from Mahmud ibn Labid, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the chiefs (nuqabaʾ): 'You are guarantors over your people, like the guarantee of the disciples for Jesus, son of Mary, and I am the guarantor of my people.' They said: 'Yes.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿So We supported those who believed﴾ that he said: "We strengthened those who believed." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him: ﴿So We supported those who believed with Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community against their enemy, so they became dominant today.﴾

It was also said that it is neither a verb of dispraise nor a verb of amazement, but rather it is predicated of "an taqulu," and "maqtan" is a specification transferred from the agent.

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row, as if they were a solid structure﴾: The commentators said: the believers said, "We wish that Allah would inform us of the deeds most beloved to Him so that we may do them, even if our wealth and our lives are lost in them." So Allah revealed ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight﴾ and so on. "Saffan" is accusative as a verbal noun, and the object is omitted, meaning: they arrange themselves in a row. It was also said that it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: lined up or arranged.

The majority read "yuqatilun" with the active voice. Zayd ibn ʿAli read it in the passive voice. It was also read "yaqtulun" with a shadda. The clause ﴿as if they were a solid structure﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of "yuqatilun," or to the pronoun in "saffan," on the assumption that it is interpreted as "lined up" or "arranged." The meaning of "marsus" is: adhering to one another; it is said, "I laid the building, I lay it with laying (rassan)," when one joins its parts to one another. Al-Farra' said: "marsus" means "with lead" (al-rasas). Al-Mubarrad said: it is derived from "I laid the building" when I plastered between its parts and brought them close until it became like a single piece. It was also said: it is from al-rasis, which is joining things to one another; and al-tarassus means adhering closely.

﴿And when Musa said to his people﴾: When He, glorified is He, mentioned that He loves those who fight in His cause, He made clear that Musa and ʿIsa commanded monotheism, strove in the cause of Allah, and punishment befell those who opposed them. The adverbial phrase is connected to an omitted verb which is "udhkur" (remember), meaning: remember, O Muhammad, for these averse people, the time when Musa spoke. It is possible that the reason for mentioning the story of Musa and ʿIsa after the love of those who strive in the cause of Allah is to warn the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) not to do with their Prophet what the people of Musa and ʿIsa did with them both. ﴿O my people, why do you harm me?﴾ This is the content of the saying: why do you harm me by opposing what I command you of the laws which Allah has made obligatory upon you? Or: why do you harm me with insults and disparagement? Among this is their accusation against him of having the "udra" (a swelling of the testicles), and the explanation of this has already been given in Surat al-Ahzab. The clause ﴿and you know that I am the Messenger of Allah to you﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, and "qad" is for the certainty of knowledge or for its emphasis. The present form signifies continuity, and the meaning is: how do you harm me while you know that I am the Messenger of Allah? A messenger is to be respected and honored, and there remains with you no doubt about the message, because of the miracles you have witnessed, which oblige you to acknowledge my message and give you certain knowledge of it.

﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾: That is, when they persisted in deviation and continued upon it, Allah caused their hearts to deviate from guidance and turned them away from accepting the truth. It was also said: when they deviated from faith, Allah caused their hearts to deviate from reward.
Muqatil said: when they turned away from the truth, Allah inclined their hearts away from it, meaning that when they abandoned the truth by harming their Prophet, Allah inclined their hearts away from the truth as a recompense for what they had committed. ﴿And Allah does not guide the corrupt people﴾: this sentence confirms the content of what precedes it.
al-Zajjaj said: He does not guide those whom it has been foreknown in His knowledge are corrupt. The meaning is that He does not guide every person characterized by corruption, and these are among them.

﴿And when ʿIsa, son of Maryam, said﴾: This is coordinated with "and when Musa said," and is governed by its own governing element, or by an omitted governing element coordinated with the governing element of the first temporal adverb.
﴿O Children of Israel, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah﴾: That is, I am the Messenger of Allah to you with the Gospel, confirming what came before me of the Torah, because I have not brought you anything that contradicts the Torah; rather it contains good tidings of me. So how can you turn away from me and oppose me? "Musaddiqan" is accusative as a circumstantial clause, and likewise "mubashshiran," and the governing element in both is the sense of sending contained in "rasul." The meaning is: I have been sent to you while confirming what came before me of the Torah and giving good tidings of one who comes after me. Since I am such in confirming and giving good tidings, there is no reason for you to deny me. "Ahmad" is the name of our Prophet (ﷺ), and it is a proper name derived from the adjective. It may be an intensive form of the active participle, meaning that he is more praising of Allah than others, or of the passive participle, meaning that he is praised for the good qualities within him more than others are praised.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, al-Sulami, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿min baʿdi﴾ with a fatha on the ya'. The rest read it with a sukun.

﴿So when he came to them with clear proofs, they said, "This is manifest magic"﴾: That is, when ʿIsa came to them with miracles, they said, "This which he has brought us is manifest, clear magic." It was also said that the intended person is Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning that when he came to them with that, they uttered this statement, and the first is preferable.

The majority read ﴿siḥrun﴾ (magic). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "sahir" (sorcerer).

﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents falsehood against Allah while he is being invited to Islam?﴾: That is, there is no one more unjust than him, since he fabricates lies against Allah while being invited to the religion of Islam, which is the best and most noble of religions. For whoever is in this condition, it is his duty not to fabricate falsehood against others, so how could he fabricate it against his Lord?

The majority read ﴿wa-huwa yudʿa﴾ from "du'a'" (invitation), in the passive voice. Talhah ibn Musarrif read "yaddaʿi" with a fatha on the ya' and a shadda on the dal, from "ida'" (claim), in the active voice. It takes "ila" because it is implicitly construed with the meaning of affiliation and belonging. ﴿And Allah does not guide the unjust people﴾: this sentence confirms the content of what precedes it. The meaning is: He does not guide one who is characterized by injustice, and those mentioned are among them.

﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths﴾: Ițfa' (extinguishing) means quenching, and its origin is with fire; it is used figuratively for what is similar to it in terms of becoming manifest. By "the light of Allah" is meant the Qur'an, meaning: they wish to nullify it and deny it by speech; or Islam; or Muhammad (ﷺ); or the proofs and evidences; or all of what has been mentioned. The meaning of "with their mouths" is: with their statements issuing from their mouths, containing reproach. ﴿But Allah will perfect His light﴾ by making it manifest throughout the horizons and elevating it above others.

Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿mutimmu nurihi﴾ with the genitive construction (idafa), and the rest read "mutimmun" with tanwin. ﴿Although the disbelievers dislike it﴾: that is, it is certainly going to happen, and the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: the lam in ﴿li-yuṭfi'ū﴾ is an emphatic lam which has entered upon the object, because the underlying form is "they wish that they extinguish." This lam is most often required when the object is fronted, as in your saying, "Lazaydun darabtu" and "Lirru'yatuka qasadtu." It was also said that it is the lam of cause, and the object is omitted, meaning: they wish to nullify the Qur'an, or to repel Islam, or to kill the Messenger, in order that they may extinguish. It was also said that it is in the sense of "an" (that), which is itself the governing particle.

al-Farra' said: the Arabs make the lam of "kay" (in order that) in the position of "an" after "arada" (wished) and "amara" (commanded). Al-Kisa'i went to this view, and similar to this is His saying: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 26].

The sentence ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, to make it prevail over all religion, even though the polytheists dislike it﴾ is a resumptive sentence confirming what precedes it. "Al-huda" is the Qur'an or the miracles. The meaning of "the religion of truth" is the true creed, which is the creed of Islam. The meaning of "li-yuzhirahu" is: to make it manifest over all religions, dominant over them and prevailing over them. ﴿Although the polytheists dislike it﴾: that is certainly going to happen.

Mujahid said: this will be when ʿIsa descends; there will be no religion on the earth except the religion of Islam. "Din" is a verbal noun used to refer to the many religions. The apodosis of "law" in both places is omitted, and the estimated reading is: He will perfect it and make it manifest.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Some of the believers, before jihad was enjoined, used to say: "We wish that Allah would inform us of the deeds most beloved to Him so that we may act upon it." So Allah informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that the most beloved deed is faith in Allah without doubt, and striving against the people of His disobedience who opposed faith and did not acknowledge it. When fighting was enjoined, some of the believers disliked it and found its command difficult, so Allah said: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿Greatly hateful in the sight of Allah is that you say what you do not do﴾, that he said: this verse concerns fighting alone, and they were people who used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and a man would say, "I fought and struck with my sword," when they had not done so; so this was revealed.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him, who said: They said, "If we knew the deeds most beloved to Allah, we would do them." So Allah informed them, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row, as if they were a solid structure﴾. They disliked that, so Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ and ﴿Greatly hateful in the sight of Allah is that you say what you do not do.﴾

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: ﴿as if they were a solid structure﴾, he said: firmly established, not moving, its parts joined closely to one another.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 61, verses 1–14 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I have names: I am Muhammad, I am Ahmad, I am al-Hashir (the Gatherer) at whose feet Allah will gather the people, I am al-Mahi (the Eraser) through whom Allah erases disbelief, and I am al-Aqib (the Last), after whom there is no prophet.'"

﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ ﴿You believe in Allah and His Messenger and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives. That is best for you, if you only knew.﴾ ﴿He will forgive you your sins and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence. That is the great achievement.﴾ ﴿And [there is] another [favor] you love: victory from Allah and an imminent conquest. So give good tidings to the believers.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, be helpers of Allah, as Jesus, the son of Mary, said to the disciples, "Who are my helpers for Allah?" The disciples said, "We are helpers of Allah." So a faction of the Children of Israel believed, and a faction disbelieved. Then We supported those who believed against their enemy, and they became dominant.﴾

His saying ﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾: He made the mentioned action equivalent to a transaction, because they profit from it just as they profit from trade, namely by their entry into Paradise and their deliverance from the Fire.

The majority of readers recited ﴿tunjikum﴾ (will save you) with light stress, from al-injaʾ (deliverance). Al-Hasan, Ibn ʿAmir and Abu Haywah recited it with emphatic stress, from al-tanjiyah.

Then Allah, glorified is He, explained this transaction to which He had pointed, saying: ﴿You believe in Allah and His Messenger and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives.﴾ This is a statement in the sense of a command, to indicate the obligation of compliance, so it is as though it has already occurred, and so He informed of its occurrence. He placed mention of wealth before lives because it is that with which one begins in spending and in preparing for jihad.

The majority recited ﴿tuʾminūna﴾ (you believe), while Ibn Masʿud recited: "Āminū wa-jāhidū" (believe and strive), in the imperative.

Al-Akhfash said: ﴿tuʾminūna﴾ is a explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayān) to "tijarah" (transaction). The better view is that the clause is a new sentence (mustaʾnafah) explaining what precedes it. The demonstrative in His saying ﴿dhālikum﴾ (that) refers to the mentioned belief and jihad; it is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿khayrun lakum﴾ (is best for you), meaning: this act is better for you than your wealth and your lives. ﴿If you [only] knew﴾ means: if you are among those who know, for you would know that it is best for you; not if you are of the people of ignorance, for then you would not know that.

﴿He will forgive you your sins﴾: This is the answer to the command implied by the wording of the statement, and for this reason it is in the jussive mood.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Mubarrad said: His saying ﴿tuʾminūna﴾ has the meaning of "āminū" (believe!), and for this reason ﴿yaghfir lakum﴾ (He will forgive you) came in the jussive mood.

Al-Farraʾ said: ﴿yaghfir lakum﴾ is the answer to the interrogative, so he made it jussive because it is the answer to the interrogative. The scholars have considered this an error.

Al-Zajjaj said: When He directs them to what benefits them, it is not that He forgives them; rather He forgives them when they believe and strive.

Al-Razi, in explaining al-Farraʾ's view, said: "Hal adullukum" (shall I guide you?) has the meaning of a command in his view, as one says "Hal anta sakit?" (Are you silent?), meaning "be silent!" Its explanation is that "hal" has the meaning of interrogation, then it gradually becomes an offer and an urging, and urging is like incitement, and incitement is a command.

Zayd ibn ʿAli recited "tuʾminū, wa-tujāhidū" (believe and strive), with the imperative particle lam elided and understood.

It was also said: "yaghfir lakum" is jussive by an implied condition, meaning: if you believe, He will forgive you. Some recited with assimilation (idgham) in ﴿yaghfir lakum﴾, but the better course is to omit assimilation, because the rāʾ is a repeated letter, so it is not good to assimilate it into the lām.

﴿And He will admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾: The manner of the rivers flowing beneath the gardens has already been explained. ﴿And pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence﴾: that is, in gardens of lasting abode. ﴿That is the great achievement﴾: that is, the mentioned forgiveness and the admission into the described gardens is the achievement after which there is no further achievement, and the triumph to which none is comparable.

﴿And [there is] another [favor] you love﴾

Al-Akhfash and al-Farraʾ said: "ukhrā" (another) is in conjunction with "tijarah" (transaction), so it is in the genitive position; that is, "shall I guide you to another quality you love, in this world along with the reward of the Hereafter?" It was also said it is in the nominative position, meaning "and for you is another quality," and it was said it is in the accusative position, meaning "and He will give you another quality."

Then Allah, glorified is He, explained this other [favor], saying: ﴿victory from Allah and an imminent conquest﴾: that is, it is victory from Allah for you and an imminent conquest.

Al-Kalbi said: it means victory over Quraysh and the conquest of Makkah.

ʿAta' said: it means the conquest of Persia and Byzantium. ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ is conjoined to an omitted element, meaning: say, O you who have believed, and give good tidings; or it is conjoined to "tuʾminūna," since it has the meaning of a command. The meaning is: give good tidings, O Muhammad, to the believers of victory and conquest; or give them good tidings of victory in this world and conquest, and of Paradise in the Hereafter; or give them good tidings of Paradise in the Hereafter.

Then Allah, glorified is He, urged the believers to support His religion, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, be helpers of Allah﴾: that is, persist in what you are upon of supporting the religion.

Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Nafi' recited "anṣāran lillāh" with tanwin and without the idafah (construct). The rest recited with the idafah. The orthography admits both readings together, and Abu ʿUbayd chose the reading with idafah because of His saying ﴿We are helpers of Allah﴾ with the idafah.

﴿As Jesus, the son of Mary, said to the disciples, "Who are my helpers for Allah?"﴾: that is, support the religion of Allah in the manner of the support of the disciples when Jesus said to them, "Who are my helpers for Allah?" They said, "We are helpers of Allah." The kaf in "kamā qāla" is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, its estimate being: "be a being like what he said." It was also said the kaf is in the accusative position by an implied verb. It was also said it is a statement carried on its meaning rather than its wording, and the meaning is: be helpers of Allah as the disciples were helpers of Jesus when he said to them, "Who are my helpers for Allah?"

His saying ﴿ilā Allāh﴾ (for Allah): it was said "ilā" has the meaning of "maʿa" (with), that is, "who are my helpers with Allah?" It was said the estimate is: "who are my helpers in what brings one closer to Allah?" It was said the estimate is: "who are my helpers heading toward the support of Allah?" The discussion of this has already preceded in Surat Al ʿImran.

The disciples (al-Hawariyyun) were the helpers of the Messiah and his pure companions, and the first to believe in him; their description has already preceded.

﴿So a faction of the Children of Israel believed and a faction disbelieved﴾: that is, a faction believed in Jesus and a faction disbelieved in him. That was because, when they differed after his raising, they separated and fought. ﴿Then We supported those who believed against their enemy﴾: that is, We strengthened the righteous among them against the falsifiers. ﴿So they became dominant﴾: that is, high and victorious. It was said the meaning is: We then supported the Muslims against both factions together.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: They said, "If only we knew which deeds are most beloved to Allah!" So there was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ They disliked it, so there was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ up to His saying: ﴿a solid structure﴾.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, be helpers of Allah﴾ that he said: "That has already occurred, praise be to Allah. Seventy men came to him, pledged allegiance to him at al-ʿAqabah, sheltered him and supported him, until Allah made His religion prevail."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Saʿd narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAmr ibn Hazm, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the group who met him at al-ʿAqabah: 'Bring out to me twelve of you who will be guarantors over their people, as the disciples were guarantors for Jesus, son of Mary.'"

Ibn Saʿd narrated from Mahmud ibn Labid, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the chiefs (nuqabaʾ): 'You are guarantors over your people, like the guarantee of the disciples for Jesus, son of Mary, and I am the guarantor of my people.' They said: 'Yes.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿So We supported those who believed﴾ that he said: "We strengthened those who believed." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him: ﴿So We supported those who believed with Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community against their enemy, so they became dominant today.﴾

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 61, verses 1–14 (part 1 of 2):

It is Madani (revealed in Medina).
Al-Mawardi said: this is the view of the majority.
Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surat al-Saff was revealed in Medina."
Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.
Al-Nahhas narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surat al-Saff was revealed in Mecca." Perhaps this is not authentic from him. What supports its being Madani is what Ahmad narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, who said: "We were discussing among ourselves which of us would go to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and ask him: 'Which deeds are most beloved to Allah?' None of us stood up. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent for us one by one and gathered us, and he recited to us this surah, meaning Surat al-Saff, in its entirety." Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated it, and said at its end: "So this surah was revealed concerning them."
al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim also narrated it, and al-Hakim said: "Sahih according to the criteria of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim)." al-Bayhaqi also narrated it in al-Shuʿab and al-Sunan.

(p-1487) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah﴾: this has already been discussed. The reason some surahs use the present tense and others the imperative is to direct attention to the legitimacy of glorifying (tasbih) at all times, past, future and present, and we have already mentioned something similar at the beginning of Surat al-Hadid. ﴿And He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾: al-ʿAziz means the Overpowering who cannot be overpowered, and al-Hakim means the Wise in His acts and His words.

﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ This interrogative is for reproach and rebuke, meaning: why do you say good things that you do not do? "Lima" is composed of the preposition lam (li-) and the interrogative "ma," and its alif was dropped for lightness because of its frequent use, as in its counterparts.

Then He, glorified is He, censured them for this, saying: ﴿Greatly hateful in the sight of Allah is that you say what you do not do﴾. That is: this is greatly abhorrent in terms of hatred (maqt), which is aversion. Al-maqt and al-maqatah are both verbal nouns. It is said: "a man is maqit and mamqut" when people do not love him. Al-Kisa'i said: "an tqulu" is in the position of nominative, because "kabura" is a verb with the meaning of "baisa" (how wretched), and "maqtan" is accusative as a specification (tamyiz). On this view, "kabura" contains an ambiguous pronoun explained by the indefinite noun, and "an taqulu" is the subject of the dispraise. There arises the disagreement over whether its nominative is by inception (mubtada'), with its predicate being the sentence preceding it, or whether its predicate is omitted, or whether it is the predicate of an omitted subject.

It was also said that it is neither a verb of dispraise nor a verb of amazement, but rather it is predicated of "an taqulu," and "maqtan" is a specification transferred from the agent.

So Allah revealed ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight﴾ and so on. "Saffan" is accusative as a verbal noun, and the object is omitted, meaning: they arrange themselves in a row. It was also said that it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: lined up or arranged.

The clause ﴿as if they were a solid structure﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of "yuqatilun," or to the pronoun in "saffan," on the assumption that it is interpreted as "lined up" or "arranged." Al-Farra' said: "marsus" means "with lead" (al-rasas). Al-Mubarrad said: it is derived from "I laid the building" when I plastered between its parts and brought them close until it became like a single piece. It was also said: it is from al-rasis, which is joining things to one another; and al-tarassus means adhering closely.

﴿And when Musa said to his people﴾: When He, glorified is He, mentioned that He loves those who fight in His cause, He made clear that Musa and ʿIsa commanded monotheism, strove in the cause of Allah, and punishment befell those who opposed them. The adverbial phrase is connected to an omitted verb which is "udhkur" (remember), meaning: remember, O Muhammad, for these averse people, the time when Musa spoke. It is possible that the reason for mentioning the story of Musa and ʿIsa after the love of those who strive in the cause of Allah is to warn the community of Muhammad (ﷺ) not to do with their Prophet what the people of Musa and ʿIsa did with them both. ﴿O my people, why do you harm me?﴾ This is the content of the saying: why do you harm me by opposing what I command you of the laws which Allah has made obligatory upon you? Or: why do you harm me with insults and disparagement? Among this is their accusation against him of having the "udra" (a swelling of the testicles), and the explanation of this has already been given in Surat al-Ahzab. The clause ﴿and you know that I am the Messenger of Allah to you﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause, and "qad" is for the certainty of knowledge or for its emphasis. The present form signifies continuity, and the meaning is: how do you harm me while you know that I am the Messenger of Allah? A messenger is to be respected and honored, and there remains with you no doubt about the message, because of the miracles you have witnessed, which oblige you to acknowledge my message and give you certain knowledge of it.

﴿So when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate﴾: That is, when they persisted in deviation and continued upon it, Allah caused their hearts to deviate from guidance and turned them away from accepting the truth. It was also said: when they deviated from faith, Allah caused their hearts to deviate from reward.

al-Zajjaj said: He does not guide those whom it has been foreknown in His knowledge are corrupt. The meaning is that He does not guide every person characterized by corruption, and these are among them.

﴿And when ʿIsa, son of Maryam, said﴾: This is coordinated with "and when Musa said," and is governed by its own governing element, or by an omitted governing element coordinated with the governing element of the first temporal adverb.
﴿O Children of Israel, indeed I am the Messenger of Allah to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah﴾: That is, I am the Messenger of Allah to you with the Gospel, confirming what came before me of the Torah, because I have not brought you anything that contradicts the Torah; rather it contains good tidings of me. So how can you turn away from me and oppose me? "Musaddiqan" is accusative as a circumstantial clause, and likewise "mubashshiran," and the governing element in both is the sense of sending contained in "rasul." The meaning is: I have been sent to you while confirming what came before me of the Torah and giving good tidings of one who comes after me. Since I am such in confirming and giving good tidings, there is no reason for you to deny me. "Ahmad" is the name of our Prophet (ﷺ), and it is a proper name derived from the adjective. It may be an intensive form of the active participle, meaning that he is more praising of Allah than others, or of the passive participle, meaning that he is praised for the good qualities within him more than others are praised.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, al-Sulami, Zirr ibn Hubaysh, and Abu Bakr from ʿAsim read ﴿min baʿdi﴾ with a fatha on the ya'. The rest read it with a sukun.

﴿So when he came to them with clear proofs, they said, "This is manifest magic"﴾: That is, when ʿIsa came to them with miracles, they said, "This which he has brought us is manifest, clear magic." It was also said that the intended person is Muhammad (ﷺ), meaning that when he came to them with that, they uttered this statement, and the first is preferable.

The majority read ﴿siḥrun﴾ (magic). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "sahir" (sorcerer).

﴿And who is more unjust than one who invents falsehood against Allah while he is being invited to Islam?﴾: That is, there is no one more unjust than him, since he fabricates lies against Allah while being invited to the religion of Islam, which is the best and most noble of religions. For whoever is in this condition, it is his duty not to fabricate falsehood against others, so how could he fabricate it against his Lord?

The majority read ﴿wa-huwa yudʿa﴾ from "du'a'" (invitation), in the passive voice. Talhah ibn Musarrif read "yaddaʿi" with a fatha on the ya' and a shadda on the dal, from "ida'" (claim), in the active voice. It takes "ila" because it is implicitly construed with the meaning of affiliation and belonging. ﴿And Allah does not guide the unjust people﴾: this sentence confirms the content of what precedes it. The meaning is: He does not guide one who is characterized by injustice, and those mentioned are among them.

﴿They wish to extinguish the light of Allah with their mouths﴾: Ițfa' (extinguishing) means quenching, and its origin is with fire; it is used figuratively for what is similar to it in terms of becoming manifest. By "the light of Allah" is meant the Qur'an, meaning: they wish to nullify it and deny it by speech; or Islam; or Muhammad (ﷺ); or the proofs and evidences; or all of what has been mentioned. The meaning of "with their mouths" is: with their statements issuing from their mouths, containing reproach. ﴿But Allah will perfect His light﴾ by making it manifest throughout the horizons and elevating it above others.

Ibn Kathir, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from ʿAsim read ﴿mutimmu nurihi﴾ with the genitive construction (idafa), and the rest read "mutimmun" with tanwin. ﴿Although the disbelievers dislike it﴾: that is, it is certainly going to happen, and the clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause.

Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: the lam in ﴿li-yuṭfi'ū﴾ is an emphatic lam which has entered upon the object, because the underlying form is "they wish that they extinguish." This lam is most often required when the object is fronted, as in your saying, "Lazaydun darabtu" and "Lirru'yatuka qasadtu." It was also said that it is the lam of cause, and the object is omitted, meaning: they wish to nullify the Qur'an, or to repel Islam, or to kill the Messenger, in order that they may extinguish. It was also said that it is in the sense of "an" (that), which is itself the governing particle.

al-Farra' said: the Arabs make the lam of "kay" (in order that) in the position of "an" after "arada" (wished) and "amara" (commanded). Al-Kisa'i went to this view, and similar to this is His saying: ﴿Allah desires to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa': 26].

The sentence ﴿It is He who sent His Messenger with guidance and the religion of truth, to make it prevail over all religion, even though the polytheists dislike it﴾ is a resumptive sentence confirming what precedes it. "Al-huda" is the Qur'an or the miracles. The meaning of "the religion of truth" is the true creed, which is the creed of Islam. The meaning of "li-yuzhirahu" is: to make it manifest over all religions, dominant over them and prevailing over them. ﴿Although the polytheists dislike it﴾: that is certainly going to happen.

Mujahid said: this will be when ʿIsa descends; there will be no religion on the earth except the religion of Islam. "Din" is a verbal noun used to refer to the many religions. The apodosis of "law" in both places is omitted, and the estimated reading is: He will perfect it and make it manifest.

Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Some of the believers, before jihad was enjoined, used to say: "We wish that Allah would inform us of the deeds most beloved to Him so that we may act upon it." So Allah informed His Prophet (ﷺ) that the most beloved deed is faith in Allah without doubt, and striving against the people of His disobedience who opposed faith and did not acknowledge it. When fighting was enjoined, some of the believers disliked it and found its command difficult, so Allah said: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾

Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿Greatly hateful in the sight of Allah is that you say what you do not do﴾, that he said: this verse concerns fighting alone, and they were people who used to come to the Prophet (ﷺ) and a man would say, "I fought and struck with my sword," when they had not done so; so this was revealed.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn Mardawayh also narrated from him, who said: They said, "If we knew the deeds most beloved to Allah, we would do them." So Allah informed them, saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row, as if they were a solid structure﴾. They disliked that, so Allah revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ and ﴿Greatly hateful in the sight of Allah is that you say what you do not do.﴾

Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him: ﴿as if they were a solid structure﴾, he said: firmly established, not moving, its parts joined closely to one another.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 61, verses 1–14 (part 2 of 2):

Al-Bukhari, Muslim and others narrated from Jubayr ibn Mut'im, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'I have names: I am Muhammad, I am Ahmad, I am al-Hashir (the Gatherer) at whose feet Allah will gather the people, I am al-Mahi (the Eraser) through whom Allah erases disbelief, and I am al-Aqib (the Last), after whom there is no prophet.'"

﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ ﴿You believe in Allah and His Messenger and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives. That is best for you, if you only knew.﴾ ﴿He will forgive you your sins and admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence. That is the great achievement.﴾ ﴿And [there is] another [favor] you love: victory from Allah and an imminent conquest. So give good tidings to the believers.﴾ ﴿O you who have believed, be helpers of Allah, as Jesus, the son of Mary, said to the disciples, "Who are my helpers for Allah?" The disciples said, "We are helpers of Allah." So a faction of the Children of Israel believed, and a faction disbelieved. Then We supported those who believed against their enemy, and they became dominant.﴾

His saying ﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾: He made the mentioned action equivalent to a transaction, because they profit from it just as they profit from trade, namely by their entry into Paradise and their deliverance from the Fire.

The majority of readers recited ﴿tunjikum﴾ (will save you) with light stress, from al-injaʾ (deliverance). Al-Hasan, Ibn ʿAmir and Abu Haywah recited it with emphatic stress, from al-tanjiyah.

Then Allah, glorified is He, explained this transaction to which He had pointed, saying: ﴿You believe in Allah and His Messenger and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives.﴾ This is a statement in the sense of a command, to indicate the obligation of compliance, so it is as though it has already occurred, and so He informed of its occurrence. He placed mention of wealth before lives because it is that with which one begins in spending and in preparing for jihad.

The majority recited ﴿tuʾminūna﴾ (you believe), while Ibn Masʿud recited: "Āminū wa-jāhidū" (believe and strive), in the imperative.

Al-Akhfash said: ﴿tuʾminūna﴾ is a explanatory apposition (ʿatf bayān) to "tijarah" (transaction). The better view is that the clause is a new sentence (mustaʾnafah) explaining what precedes it. The demonstrative in His saying ﴿dhālikum﴾ (that) refers to the mentioned belief and jihad; it is the subject, and its predicate is ﴿khayrun lakum﴾ (is best for you), meaning: this act is better for you than your wealth and your lives. ﴿If you [only] knew﴾ means: if you are among those who know, for you would know that it is best for you; not if you are of the people of ignorance, for then you would not know that.

﴿He will forgive you your sins﴾: This is the answer to the command implied by the wording of the statement, and for this reason it is in the jussive mood.

Al-Zajjaj and al-Mubarrad said: His saying ﴿tuʾminūna﴾ has the meaning of "āminū" (believe!), and for this reason ﴿yaghfir lakum﴾ (He will forgive you) came in the jussive mood.

Al-Farraʾ said: ﴿yaghfir lakum﴾ is the answer to the interrogative, so he made it jussive because it is the answer to the interrogative. The scholars have considered this an error.

Al-Zajjaj said: When He directs them to what benefits them, it is not that He forgives them; rather He forgives them when they believe and strive.

Al-Razi, in explaining al-Farraʾ's view, said: "Hal adullukum" (shall I guide you?) has the meaning of a command in his view, as one says "Hal anta sakit?" (Are you silent?), meaning "be silent!" Its explanation is that "hal" has the meaning of interrogation, then it gradually becomes an offer and an urging, and urging is like incitement, and incitement is a command.

Zayd ibn ʿAli recited "tuʾminū, wa-tujāhidū" (believe and strive), with the imperative particle lam elided and understood.

It was also said: "yaghfir lakum" is jussive by an implied condition, meaning: if you believe, He will forgive you. Some recited with assimilation (idgham) in ﴿yaghfir lakum﴾, but the better course is to omit assimilation, because the rāʾ is a repeated letter, so it is not good to assimilate it into the lām.

﴿And He will admit you to gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾: The manner of the rivers flowing beneath the gardens has already been explained. ﴿And pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence﴾: that is, in gardens of lasting abode. ﴿That is the great achievement﴾: that is, the mentioned forgiveness and the admission into the described gardens is the achievement after which there is no further achievement, and the triumph to which none is comparable.

﴿And [there is] another [favor] you love﴾

Al-Akhfash and al-Farraʾ said: "ukhrā" (another) is in conjunction with "tijarah" (transaction), so it is in the genitive position; that is, "shall I guide you to another quality you love, in this world along with the reward of the Hereafter?" It was also said it is in the nominative position, meaning "and for you is another quality," and it was said it is in the accusative position, meaning "and He will give you another quality."

Then Allah, glorified is He, explained this other [favor], saying: ﴿victory from Allah and an imminent conquest﴾: that is, it is victory from Allah for you and an imminent conquest.

Al-Kalbi said: it means victory over Quraysh and the conquest of Makkah.

ʿAta' said: it means the conquest of Persia and Byzantium. ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ is conjoined to an omitted element, meaning: say, O you who have believed, and give good tidings; or it is conjoined to "tuʾminūna," since it has the meaning of a command. The meaning is: give good tidings, O Muhammad, to the believers of victory and conquest; or give them good tidings of victory in this world and conquest, and of Paradise in the Hereafter; or give them good tidings of Paradise in the Hereafter.

Then Allah, glorified is He, urged the believers to support His religion, saying: ﴿O you who have believed, be helpers of Allah﴾: that is, persist in what you are upon of supporting the religion.

Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr and Nafi' recited "anṣāran lillāh" with tanwin and without the idafah (construct). The rest recited with the idafah. The orthography admits both readings together, and Abu ʿUbayd chose the reading with idafah because of His saying ﴿We are helpers of Allah﴾ with the idafah.

﴿As Jesus, the son of Mary, said to the disciples, "Who are my helpers for Allah?"﴾: that is, support the religion of Allah in the manner of the support of the disciples when Jesus said to them, "Who are my helpers for Allah?" They said, "We are helpers of Allah." The kaf in "kamā qāla" is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, its estimate being: "be a being like what he said." It was also said the kaf is in the accusative position by an implied verb. It was also said it is a statement carried on its meaning rather than its wording, and the meaning is: be helpers of Allah as the disciples were helpers of Jesus when he said to them, "Who are my helpers for Allah?"

His saying ﴿ilā Allāh﴾ (for Allah): it was said "ilā" has the meaning of "maʿa" (with), that is, "who are my helpers with Allah?" It was said the estimate is: "who are my helpers in what brings one closer to Allah?" It was said the estimate is: "who are my helpers heading toward the support of Allah?" The discussion of this has already preceded in Surat Al ʿImran.

The disciples (al-Hawariyyun) were the helpers of the Messiah and his pure companions, and the first to believe in him; their description has already preceded.

﴿So a faction of the Children of Israel believed and a faction disbelieved﴾: that is, a faction believed in Jesus and a faction disbelieved in him. That was because, when they differed after his raising, they separated and fought. ﴿Then We supported those who believed against their enemy﴾: that is, We strengthened the righteous among them against the falsifiers. ﴿So they became dominant﴾: that is, high and victorious. It was said the meaning is: We then supported the Muslims against both factions together.

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: They said, "If only we knew which deeds are most beloved to Allah!" So there was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, shall I guide you to a transaction that will save you from a painful punishment?﴾ They disliked it, so there was revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ up to His saying: ﴿a solid structure﴾.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatadah regarding His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, be helpers of Allah﴾ that he said: "That has already occurred, praise be to Allah. Seventy men came to him, pledged allegiance to him at al-ʿAqabah, sheltered him and supported him, until Allah made His religion prevail."

Ibn Ishaq and Ibn Saʿd narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Abi Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAmr ibn Hazm, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the group who met him at al-ʿAqabah: 'Bring out to me twelve of you who will be guarantors over their people, as the disciples were guarantors for Jesus, son of Mary.'"

Ibn Saʿd narrated from Mahmud ibn Labid, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to the chiefs (nuqabaʾ): 'You are guarantors over your people, like the guarantee of the disciples for Jesus, son of Mary, and I am the guarantor of my people.' They said: 'Yes.'"

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas regarding ﴿So We supported those who believed﴾ that he said: "We strengthened those who believed." Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him: ﴿So We supported those who believed with Muhammad (ﷺ) and his community against their enemy, so they became dominant today.﴾

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 61, verses 1–14 (part 1 of 2):

It is Madani (revealed in Medina).
Al-Mawardi said: this is the view of the majority.
Ibn al-Durays, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surat al-Saff was revealed in Medina."
Ibn Mardawayh narrated the same from Ibn al-Zubayr.
Al-Nahhas narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "Surat al-Saff was revealed in Mecca." Perhaps this is not authentic from him. What supports its being Madani is what Ahmad narrated from ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam, who said: "We were discussing among ourselves which of us would go to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and ask him: 'Which deeds are most beloved to Allah?' None of us stood up. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent for us one by one and gathered us, and he recited to us this surah, meaning Surat al-Saff, in its entirety." Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated it, and said at its end: "So this surah was revealed concerning them."
al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Hibban, and al-Hakim also narrated it, and al-Hakim said: "Sahih according to the criteria of the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim)." al-Bayhaqi also narrated it in al-Shuʿab and al-Sunan.

(p-1487) In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

His saying ﴿Whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth glorifies Allah﴾: this has already been discussed. The reason some surahs use the present tense and others the imperative is to direct attention to the legitimacy of glorifying (tasbih) at all times, past, future and present, and we have already mentioned something similar at the beginning of Surat al-Hadid. ﴿And He is the Mighty, the Wise﴾: al-ʿAziz means the Overpowering who cannot be overpowered, and al-Hakim means the Wise in His acts and His words.

﴿O you who have believed, why do you say what you do not do?﴾ This interrogative is for reproach and rebuke, meaning: why do you say good things that you do not do? "Lima" is composed of the preposition lam (li-) and the interrogative "ma," and its alif was dropped for lightness because of its frequent use, as in its counterparts.

Then He, glorified is He, censured them for this, saying: ﴿Greatly hateful in the sight of Allah is that you say what you do not do﴾. That is: this is greatly abhorrent in terms of hatred (maqt), which is aversion. Al-maqt and al-maqatah are both verbal nouns. It is said: "a man is maqit and mamqut" when people do not love him. Al-Kisa'i said: "an tqulu" is in the position of nominative, because "kabura" is a verb with the meaning of "baisa" (how wretched), and "maqtan" is accusative as a specification (tamyiz). On this view, "kabura" contains an ambiguous pronoun explained by the indefinite noun, and "an taqulu" is the subject of the dispraise. There arises the disagreement over whether its nominative is by inception (mubtada'), with its predicate being the sentence preceding it, or whether its predicate is omitted, or whether it is the predicate of an omitted subject.

If it were said that by his saying "kabura" he intended amazement (ta'ajjub), Ibn ʿUsfur counted it among the verbs of amazement.
It was also said that it is neither a verb of dispraise nor a verb of amazement, but rather it is predicated of "an taqulu," and "maqtan" is a specification transferred from the agent.

﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row, as if they were a solid structure﴾: The commentators said: the believers said, "We wish that Allah would inform us of the deeds most beloved to Him so that we may do them, even if our wealth and our lives are lost in them." So Allah revealed ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight﴾ and so on. "Saffan" is accusative as a verbal noun, and the object is omitted, meaning: they arrange themselves in a row. It was also said that it is a verbal noun in the position of a circumstantial accusative (hal), meaning: lined up or arranged.

The majority read "yuqatilun" with the active voice. Zayd ibn ʿAli read it in the passive voice. It was also read "yaqtulun" with a shadda. The clause ﴿as if they were a solid structure﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the subject of "yuqatilun," or to the pronoun in "saffan," on the assumption that it is interpreted as "lined up" or "arranged." The meaning of "marsus" is: adhering to one another; it is said, "I laid the building, I lay it with laying (rassan)," when one joins its parts to one another. Al-Farra' said: "marsus" means "with lead" (al-rasas). Al-Mubarrad said: it is derived from "I laid the building" when I plastered between its parts and brought them close until it became like a single piece. It was also said: it is from al-rasis, which is joining things to one another; and al-tarassus means adhering closely.

﴿And when Musa said to his people﴾: When He, glorified is He, mentioned that He loves those who fight in His cause, He made clear that Musa and ʿIsa commanded monotheism, strove in the cause of Allah, and punishment befell those who opposed them. The adverbial phrase is connected to an omitted verb which is "udhkur" (remember), meaning: remember, O Muhammad, for these averse people, the time when Musa spoke.
